newsitem.title: JAPAN: US car industry chief says favours 100 yen to dlr.
newsitem.headline: US car industry chief says favours 100 yen to dlr.

text.p: The leader of a major U.S. car industry group said on Wednesday that the dollar should be around 100 yen, as a weaker yen hurts U.S. car makers' competitiveness in Japan.

American Automobile Manufacturers Association president Andrew Card said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television that the dollar at 110 yen could hurt the progress Tokyo and Washington have made since reaching a bilateral car trade pact last year.
"I think the yen-dollar relationship...should be more in the neighbourhood of 100 yen per dollar," he said.
The dollar was trading at around 110.20 yen in Tokyo morning trade on Wednesday. This compares with its record low of 79.75 yen reached in April 1995.
"I think once the yen hits 110 yen per dollar, it puts a tremendous strain on the ability of GM, Ford and Chrysler to meet the expectations of Japanese consumers," he said.
He said he expected sales of American car parts in Japan to drop due to the yen's weakness.

Commenting on a remark by U.S. Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor on Tuesday that the dollar's recent strength against the yen appears not to have hurt U.S. car sales in Japan, Card said Kantor may have made "a plain mistake".
Kantor, speaking to reporters in Washington in answer to a question on the dollar's recent strength, had said: "It appears not to have had any adverse effect whatsoever on our ability to sell cars."
A strong dollar against the yen makes U.S. manufacturers less competitive in the Japanese market because it makes their products more expensive in yen terms.
"He (Kantor) is understanding our challenges... I don't think he really believes that (the statement)," Card said.
"So the 110 (yen) level is, I think, a point where we are saying 'please pay attention'. There is a lot of damage that would come as a result of this exchange rate," he said.

In June 1995, Tokyo and Washington reached a pact on opening Japan's car market to U.S. manufacturers, reaching an agreement just in time to avert punitive U.S. tariffs on imports of Japanese luxury cars.
Card said sales of American-made cars in Japan have increased over the year, but also said there was a lack of efforts by Japanese dealers to sell U.S. cars.
"Th lack of progress really has been in an area of reaching consumers. We are frustrated that more dealers have not signed up to carry American-made products," he said.
U.S. and Japanese trade officials are to meet on Wednesday and Thursday in San Francisco to review the year-old accord.
